To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Africanisation project is an exercise in futility, and that the only way forward for African psychologists is to embrace transmodernity.
the dominant indigenization discourse of psychology is a cowardly, defeatist, ahistorical and totally Eurocentric.
African psychology is a field of study that focuses on the study of the human mind and human behavior within the context of African culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how to decolonise psychology in Africa, in the sense of how to make psychology in Africa relevant to Africans, and not just to Western psychology, and how to do so in ways that do not reproduce the coloniality of power and the epistemic violence of modernism.
the politics of knowledge, and how the politics of knowledge are produced, reproduced, and resisted.
the ways in which the dominant indigenization discourse of psychology in the South African context conceives the process as equivalent to Africanization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
African psychology is a non-starter.
the indigenisation project is a failed project and should be jettisoned.
, the indigenisation of psychology in Africa, is not about the “Africanisation” of psychology, but the “psychologisation” of Africanity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper is a critique of the dominant indigenization discourse of African psychologists, and a call for a different decolonizing ethics.
we need to be wary of the pitfalls of essentialising and cultural reductionism in the indigenisation project, as well as the dangers of the modernist universalising project of psychology.
, in order to be able to move beyond modernity and modernist psychology, we need to be willing to move beyond ourselves and our own cultural particularisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the “Africanization” of psychology is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for decolonising psychology in South Africa.
the “decolonization” of modernist psychology should be a two-way process, and that it is not enough to simply “decolonize” psychology from the “West” without also decolonizing it from “Africa”.
African psychology must be more inclusive and less ethno-centric, and that it should be less defensive and more open to dialogue and collaboration with Western psychology.
